Photograph: Sergei Supinsky/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ahead of discussions in Kyiv with US President Donald Trump's envoys on Sunday. Photograph: Sergei Supinsky/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy links Russian strikes on Kyiv airports to US envoys’ visit Moscow attacked Kyiv and Boryspil international airports as talks yielded no evident change in Vladimir Putin’s peace demands. What we know on day 1,656 Guardian staff and agences Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.37 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 21.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports were “clearly” a reaction to the possibility of the US negotiators flying to Kyiv after talks in Moscow , the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.” Both airports service the Ukrainian capital. There was no comment from the US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff , who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and were ‌due to meet Zelenskyy in Kyiv ‌on Sunday. The Kremlin’s tone appeared unchanged . After three hours of talks, an aide to Vladimir Putin, Yuri Ushakov, said the Russian president had told the US pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield, was confident of achieving ⁠its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”. Ushakov said ​the Americans had “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement”, but he did not say what those ideas were. Putin begins talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ending war with Ukraine Read more The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250km (775-mile) frontline . Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. Kremlin spokesperson ‌Dmitry Peskov posted online that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Saturday. However, he said Russia had not yet agreed to a broader three-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through to Monday. Russian attacks killed five employees and wounded five others at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, said the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. “A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants that it claimed were sites for military production. A 62-year-old man was wounded, and several homes and an apartment building damaged, in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district , Hanzha said. The city of Dnipro and the nearby Pidhorodne community were among the areas hit. One person died and five other were injured, including two men who were hospitalised in serious condition. A sixth civilian was injured in an attack on the Nikopol district. Other deadly Russian attacks took place in Chuhuiv in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region , on the Bucha district of Ukraine’s Kyiv region , and on a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region . In Russia’s Belrogod region on the border with Ukraine, two people were killed and three others wounded by Ukrainian attacks on Saturday, local authorities said. Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones, Ukraine’s air force said on Saturday. https://www.mfa.gov.lv/en/article/baiba-.text: Baiba Braže and Armenian Minister of Foreign Affairs sign readmission agreement Published: 07.09.2026. Photo: Laura Celmiņa, Ministry of Foreign Affairs Facebook X / Twitter Linkedin Threads On 7 September 2026, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Baiba Braže, welcomed the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Armenia, Ararat Mirzoyan, and signed a protocol between Latvia and Armenia on the implementation of the EU-Armenia readmission agreement, which will strengthen cooperation between the two countries in combating illegal migration. The Minister expressed support for deepening relations between Armenia and the European Union (EU), as well as between Latvia and Armenia. The Ministers also discussed cooperation in the fields of ICT, digitalisation and cybersecurity, support for Ukraine, and the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan. The Minister of Foreign Affairs expressed satisfaction with the increasingly active political dialogue between Latvia and Armenia, commended Armenia’s democratic resilience and the conduct of its parliamentary elections, and highlighted Armenia’s ability to resist Russia’s destabilising influence. The Ministers discussed the rapid development of relations between Armenia and the EU. The first EU–Armenia summit took place in Yerevan in May this year, and Armenia recently hosted a meeting of the European Political Community. The Minister reaffirmed Latvia’s support for Armenia’s choice to build closer ties with Europe and its readiness to continue supporting Armenia’s reform process, including by sharing Latvia’s experience with EU integration. The EU–Armenia Resilience and Growth Plan allocates EUR 270 million to strengthen Armenia’s socioeconomic resilience, connectivity and trade, as well as to diversify its energy sector. The parties also discussed opportunities for EU–Armenia cooperation in the fields of transport, energy and digital technology. Baiba Braže and Ararat Mirzoyan agreed on the potential to expand cooperation between Latvia and Armenia in the areas of ICT, digitalisation and cybersecurity. These issues were also on the agenda during Baiba Braže’s visit to Yerevan in May, including in talks with the Minister of High-Tech Industry of Armenia. Latvia is interested in fostering closer ties between businesses and experts in the two countries. The Ministers also discussed the EU–Armenia visa liberalisation dialogue and the promotion of people-to-people contacts. Direct connectivity between the two countries is also facilitated by airBaltic’s flight between Riga and Yerevan, supporting business and tourism. When discussing Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine, Baiba Braže emphasised the need to continue strong support for Ukraine. She emphasised that the principles of international law, State sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected. Latvia continues to strengthen Ukraine’s defence capabilities and advocates continued pressure on Russia. The parties welcomed progress in the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Baiba Braže emphasised that a sustainable peace would open up new opportunities for the entire South Caucasus region in terms of transport connectivity, trade, energy and people-to-people contacts. At the conclusion of the meeting, Baiba Braže and Ararat Mirzoyan signed the Protocol between the Government of the Republic of Latvia and the Government of the Republic of Armenia on the implementation of the Agreement between the European Union and the Republic of Armenia on the readmission of persons residing without authorisation. The agreement establishes the procedures for the readmission of persons and will strengthen cooperation between the relevant authorities of Latvia and Armenia in combating illegal migration.
